paragraphs: The Sovereign has no force other than the legislative power, so it acts only by means of the laws; and since the laws are solely the authentic acts of the general will, the Sovereign cannot act except when the people is assembled. The people in assembly, I shall be told, is a mere fantasy. It is so today, but two thousand years ago it was not. Has the nature of man changed?

The limits of what is possible in moral matters are less narrow than we imagine: it is our weaknesses, our vices and our prejudices that confine them. Base souls do not believe in great men; vile slaves smile mockingly at the name of liberty.

Let us judge what can be done by what has been done. I shall say nothing of the Republics of ancient Greece; but the Roman Republic was, in my opinion, a great State, and the city of Rome a great city. The last census showed four hundred thousand citizens in Rome capable of bearing arms, and the last count of the population of the Empire showed over four million citizens, not counting subjects, foreigners, women, children and slaves.

What difficulties might one not imagine standing in the way of frequently assembling the vast population of this capital and its surroundings! Yet few weeks passed without the Roman people being assembled, and often several times. It exercised not only the rights of Sovereignty but also some of those of government. It dealt with certain matters and judged certain cases, and this whole people was found in the public meeting place almost as often as magistrates as it was as citizens.

If we went back to the earliest history of nations, we would find that most ancient governments, even those of monarchical form, such as the Macedonian and the Frankish, had similar councils. In any case, the one incontestable fact I have given answers all the difficulties; it is good logic to reason from what has actually happened to what is possible.
